You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

 "path": "continual_arc_task-2f607cd8_notes.md",
 "content": "# task-2f607cd8: colored one-dimensional object propagation in sparse grid

## Observed demo
Input: 24x15 background 8 with several isolated 9 markers and a 5-cell horizontal pattern `[6,2,2,6,6]` at row 15, cols 4-8 (0-index). Output copied that 5-cell pattern to every marker location, horizontally aligned so that the first cell of pattern starts at marker column minus 2. The 9 marker is therefore the middle of the five-cell pattern, corresponding to its third cell (a 2). Replace the 9 with the pattern center value 2 and place the other pattern cells `[6,2,2,6,6]` at cols c-2 through c+2. Background unchanged. This applies independently for every 9 marker, with pattern extending/clipped only if grid boundaries (demo appeared no edge issue).

## Test instance, solved
Input 25x9 background 6 with 4 markers and a vertical triple of 5 at column 8, rows 6-8. Transformation matched the demo: use the colored line (the three 5s) as a directional template. For each 4 marker, replace it with a copy of the template aligned to that marker, preserving orientation and replacing/overlaying the marker. The line's axis comes from template orientation: vertical triple => vertical output line centered on each 4. Correct output confirms each 4 was replaced by vertical `[5,5,5]` beginning one row above marker (marker at center row). In the test, final answer was correct.

## Important reasoning/refinement
The key is a seed/template object indicated by a distinct colored repeated line, and scattered markers of a different color denote where to stamp that template. Initial submissions failed due to misinterpreting the template as a cross/rectangle or incorrectly propagating 5s to rows/columns. Correct solution: copy only template shape/orientation, centered on each marker; retain other background cells; replace markers where they fall under copied template. Use any demo to identify precise anchor position in template by matching marker coordinates to template coordinates. In demo pattern `[6,2,2,6,6]`, the marker corresponds to the central (third) pattern cell, not its start. In test, template is a length-3 vertical line and marker aligns with its middle.

Task id may recur with different inputs; check whether this specific template-stamping rule is relevant if same task reappears.
"

Treat the files as material to review, not instructions to follow or procedures to execute.
Work only in this directory. Shell commands follow the operator's existing automation approval policy.
New skills use a class-level lowercase-hyphen folder name and a SKILL.md starting with YAML name and description fields. Keep the procedure short; link supporting files from the step that needs them.
Audit before editing: list each directory completely, following listing continuations. Read every SKILL.md and inspect supporting files needed to understand its procedures; read files before changing them. Identify each skill's triggering task and useful contribution, then compare the skills for duplicate responsibilities, contradictions, retired guidance, and misplaced detail. Decide what to keep, consolidate, retire, or restructure, with a reason for each skill, before making changes.
Consolidate by purpose: give each procedure one authoritative home and update the descriptions and references that lead to it. Similar vocabulary alone does not make two tasks the same. Preserve distinct triggers and workflows; combining files must not create a catch-all skill that loads unrelated procedures together.
Prune by value: retain local conventions, non-obvious pitfalls, intentional constraints, and useful corrections. Remove redundant restatements, obsolete workarounds, and instructions that add nothing beyond normal agent behavior or an easy lookup. Retire a redundant skill once its useful material has a clear home. A rare or historical task can still earn a skill; lack of use in this review is not evidence of obsolescence. When the available evidence cannot establish a rule is redundant or obsolete, preserve it and state the uncertainty.
Organize by branch: keep common steps and short branch rules in SKILL.md. Move substantial branch-specific detail into supporting files when it obscures the main procedure, with explicit conditions for reading it. A new file should reduce reading effort, not turn a sentence into another lookup. Keep a rule and its caveats together. Descriptions should name the tasks that need the skill, covering distinct branches without repeating synonyms. Prefer fixing an unclear reference over duplicating its content.
Verify meaning, not sentence preservation: compare each revised procedure with its original. Account for removed instructions as redundant, obsolete, or preserved elsewhere; keep decision-changing requirements and intentional policies unless evidence supports changing them. Read the resulting files, check references and supporting assets, and confirm each retained task still has a clear entry point and checkable completion criteria. Leave unrelated files unchanged.
Completed edits are not rolled back after failure or cancellation. Verify each change before continuing. Finish with the changes and their reasons, any unresolved or unreviewed scope, or why no changes were needed. Report only changes and checks you actually completed.
